1.title: Agni Named as Indra, Varuṇa, Rudra, Sarasvatī
1.synthesis:
Fifteen verses in a row open the same way — *tvam agne*, you, Agni. Across the sūkta some sixty second-person forms fall, *tvam*, *tvām*, *tava*, *tve*, and each one has a different name fastened to it. The claim being built is not that {{agni}} resembles the other gods. It is that when a god acts at the rite, the acting is Agni's.

The first verse gives the births: through the days, from the waters, from the stone, from the trees, from the plants. Five origins, and the verse ends on *śuci*, pure — whatever he is drawn out of, he comes out clean. In the middle of all that wood and water he is called *nṛpati*, lord of men.

The second verse names offices, nine of them. *Hotra*, the calling; *potra*, the purifying; *neṣṭra*, the leading; the kindler's work for the man who holds to {{ṛta}}; *praśāstra*, the directing; the *adhvaryu*'s doing; *brahmā*, who watches the whole rite and repairs it. Then the last: *gṛhapati ca no dame*, and the householder in our house. From the most specialised station in a great sacrifice down to the man who keeps a fire at home — one god holds all of it.

Then the gods themselves, four verses of them. {{indra}}, bull of the good; {{viṣṇu}} *urugāya*, wide-going, worthy of *namas*; *brahmā* who finds *rayi*, and {{brahmaṇaspati}}; the upholder joined with *puraṃdhi*, fullness of thought (v3). {{varuṇa}} whose *vrata* holds firm; {{mitra}}; {{aryaman}} the *satpati* whose bounty is shared; and {{aṃśa}}, the apportioner, dividing at the *vidatha* (v4). {{tvaṣṭṛ}}, who gives the worshipper strong sons; kinship with the *gnās*, the divine wives; the urger of swift horses; the strength of men (v5). {{rudra}}, *asura* of the great sky; the *mārutaṃ śardhas*, the {{marut}} troop itself; going with ruddy winds; and {{pūṣan}}, who guards *tmanā*, of his own accord (v6). The seventh adds the givers: Draviṇodas, who hands out substance; {{savitṛ}} the *ratnadhā*, holder of treasure; {{bhaga}}, lord of goods; and the guard in the house of whoever has served him.

At the eighth the grammar turns — *tvām*, you as object. The clans press toward Agni as *viśpati* in the house, as a king easy to find, and he outweighs tens, hundreds, thousands. The ninth is the one to remember. Men come to him as to a father; they win him to brotherhood by labour; *tvam putro bhavasi yas te avidhat* — you become a son to the one who served you; and you are a friend, kindly, who guards against assault. Father, brother, son, friend: the whole grammar of a household, and Agni takes every position in it, including the lowest.

The tenth makes him Ṛbhu and lord of *vāja*, shining, burning for the giver, and *yajñam ātaniḥ*, the one who stretches the {{yajña}} out. The eleventh gives the goddesses: {{aditi}} to the giver; {{bhāratī}}, grown by song; Iḷā of a hundred winters, for *dakṣa*; and {{sarasvatī}} — and into that line drops *vṛtrahā*, Indra's own war-name, on a list of goddesses.

The twelfth stops naming persons and names goods: highest *vayaḥ*, vitality; beauty in his colour; *vāja* that carries a man across; *rayi* broad on every side. The thirteenth and fourteenth explain why the substitutions were possible at all — the Ādityas made Agni their mouth, the pure ones made him their tongue, and through him the immortals eat what is offered, and through him mortals taste their food. He is not standing in for the gods. He is the organ they consume with. The fifteenth says he is with them and over against them by *majman*, sheer mass, and goes past them.

Then the sixteenth turns to the room: the patrons who give the singers a gift led by a cow and finished with horses — lead them and us both to what is better. *Bṛhad vadema vidathe suvīrāḥ*.
1.practice:
This is the sūkta that opens the Gṛtsamada family's own book, and where a family book begins is a decision. {{agni}} opens eight of the ten maṇḍalas — every one of the family collections, two through seven, and one and ten besides; only the eighth begins with {{indra}}, and the ninth belongs wholly to {{soma}}. Maṇḍala 2 is the shortest of the ten: 43 sūktas and 429 ṛcs out of the collection's 10,552. A small book, and it spends its first breath saying that the god at the door is also every god behind it.

That claim is the ancestor of something a Hindu does daily without naming it. The *iṣṭadevatā* — the chosen form before whom one actually sits — is not a smaller god than the rest; the tradition's position is that the one addressed contains the others. [[1.164]].46 states it as a proposition, *ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanti*, the real is one and the wise speak of it many ways. This sūkta does not argue it. It performs it, verse after verse, by refusing to stop renaming the same fire.

The second verse is worth keeping for a different reason. It runs down the roster of specialised priests — *hotā*, *potā*, *neṣṭā*, *adhvaryu*, *brahmā* — and then ends on *gṛhapati ca no dame*: and the householder in our house. The great śrauta rite needs sixteen trained men. The household needs one fire and the person who keeps it. The sūkta puts them in the same sentence and does not rank them, and that is the warrant for every domestic observance done before a lamp or a hearth by someone who is not a priest.

And verse 9 is the one to sit with. Agni is asked to be father, brother, son and friend — and *son* is not a slip. *Tvam putro bhavasi yas te avidhat*: you become a son to the one who served you. A god who has just been identified with Varuṇa and Rudra is asked, three lines later, to take the dependent position in a family. [[1.1]].9 makes the same move at the end of the collection's first hymn, asking Agni to be approachable as a father is to a son. Maṇḍala 2 opens by making the relation run both directions.
1.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa's longest note in this sūkta is on verse 2, and it is a piece of ritual bookkeeping rather than theology: the eight offices named are eight of the sixteen *ṛtvijes* of the most solemn rites, and he sets out how a *dakṣiṇā* of a hundred cows divides among four classes of four — forty-eight, twenty-four, sixteen, twelve — citing Kullūka Bhaṭṭa on Manu 8.210, with variant rosters from Aitareya Brāhmaṇa vii.1, from Rāmanātha on the Amarakośa, and from Mādhava following Kumārila.

On verse 1 he keeps two senses of *āśuśukṣaṇi*, drying up or consuming, and reads the five births concretely: Agni from the waters as lightning or as the submarine fire, from stones by striking, from wood by attrition, from plants such as bamboo rubbing in a forest.

Verse 4's *aṃśa* he takes as a form of the sun, or as the Āditya of that name; Wilson prints "a portion (of the sun)", Griffith keeps the god, "liberal Amsa in the synod". At verse 6 he glosses *asura* twice — the expeller of enemies, or the giver of strength.

Two of his glosses flatten a name into an adjective, and the translations split accordingly. At verse 10 he takes *ṛbhu* as *bhāsamāna*, shining, so Wilson has "ever resplendent" where Griffith keeps "A Rbhu art thou". At verse 11 *vṛtrahā* he reads as destroyer of sin rather than slayer of Vṛtra, and *śatahimā* as the earth of unmeasured duration.

2.title: Agni Jātavedas Kindled Nightly, Guest and King
2.synthesis:
Where [[2.1]] piled names onto {{agni}}, this sūkta watches him being tended. It opens in the imperative plural, spoken to the people at the rite rather than to the god: *yajñena vardhata jātavedasam* — increase Jātavedas, the one who knows all that is born, by the {{yajña}} itself; worship him with the offering, with continuous song. He is *samidhāna*, being kindled at this moment; *suprayas*, well fed; *hotā* at the pole where the work is done.

The second verse gives the image the hymn keeps returning to. Nights and dawns have lowed toward Agni *vatsaṃ na svasareṣu dhenavaḥ* — as milch cows in their stalls low toward the calf. The times of day want him the way an animal wants its young. And he shines through the human generations, *mānuṣā yugā*, holding steady through the dark.

Verses 3 and 4 place him. The gods set him down *budhne rajasaḥ*, at the base of the region — the lowest point of the visible world — the *arati* of heaven and earth, the one who runs between them, to be known like a famous chariot, bright-flamed, to be praised among the settlements as {{mitra}} is. Then they set him in his own house, in the vault: growing like the moon, a bird of the firmament, watching with his eyes, a guard over the ground, keeping watch toward gods and men both. Agni on the hearth and the light in the sky are being described in one breath, and neither is made a figure for the other.

The fifth verse widens him to the whole rite: let him as *hotā* go round the entire *adhvara* and enclose it. Men press toward him with offerings and with song. He is *hiriśipra*, golden-jawed, flickering among the growing plants, and he lights up the two worlds as the sky is lit by its stars.

Then the asking begins, and it is unusually concrete. Verse 6: kindled richly, shine wealth into us, make heaven and earth easy for us, so the gods may come to what men have offered. Verse 7: give greatly, give by thousands; open *vājam*, strength, like doors, so that it may be heard of; make heaven and earth favourable by *brahman*; and let the dawns break over you as the light of the sun breaks. Verse 8 returns to the daily fact underneath all of it — kindled along the nights and dawns, Agni shines out with ruddy flame, *rājā viśām atithiś cāruḥ āyave*: king of the clans, and a welcome guest to the living man. King and guest in one line, which is exactly the double position a fire holds in a house.

The ninth verse turns to the singers themselves: our *dhī*, our thought, has swelled to the immortals in the high sky, and comes back as a milch cow yielding to the poet at the rites, in hundreds, in many forms. The tenth is ambitious and says so: may we show our strength among men, by the horse or by *brahman*, and let our splendour stand high over the *pañca kṛṣṭi*, the five peoples, unsurpassable as the realm of light.

The eleventh asks Agni simply to notice — *sa no bodhi*, be aware of us — as the one to whom the well-born patrons come, who shines in his own house for offspring that will not fail. The twelfth asks that both parties, the singers and the patrons, stand inside his shelter, and that the wealth given be *prajāvat* and *svapatya*, rich in children and in good descent. And the thirteenth is the family's own closing verse, the one that will end sūkta after sūkta in this book: for the patrons who send the singers a gift headed by a cow, lead them and us to what is better — *bṛhad vadema vidathe suvīrāḥ*.
2.practice:
*Jātavedas* is the title this sūkta hands the reader in its first line and never explains, because it does not need to: the one who knows everything that has come to be. {{agni}} carries it in 128 verses of the Ṛgveda. It is the name under which he functions as witness — Agni that was present, that saw, and that therefore can be called on to attest. That is precisely the office he still holds in the saṃskāras, where Agni is not decorative but the party before whom the thing is done.

The second verse gives the image most worth carrying: the nights and dawns lowing toward Agni as cows in their stalls low toward their calves. The desire in that picture runs the wrong way for our habits — it is not the worshipper who longs, it is the times of day. Kindling at dusk and dawn is presented here not as a duty imposed on a person but as something the junctures themselves want. Anyone who keeps a lamp at sandhyā has the Ṛgvedic warrant in this verse.

The final verse is the Gṛtsamada family's signature, and it is worth knowing how distinctive it is. *Bṛhad vadema vidathe suvīrāḥ* — may we, with strong men about us, speak greatly in the assembly — closes twenty-one of maṇḍala 2's forty-three sūktas. It occurs exactly once in the other nine maṇḍalas, at [[9.86]].48, and the Anukramaṇī assigns that verse too to Śaunaka Gṛtsamada. A whole family signed its work with one line, and the line asks not for wealth but for standing: to be able to speak, well, in public, with one's people around one. The word for that gathering, *vidatha*, occurs 111 times in the Ṛgveda; 28 of those are in this shortest of the ten books.

And note what verse 10 asks for and how it hedges. May we show our strength *arvatā vā brahmaṇā vā* — by the horse, or by *brahman*, the formulated word. Force or formulation: the sūkta names both as legitimate routes to standing among the five peoples, and does not choose.
2.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa's note on verse 3 is a small, decisive piece of interpretation: *budhne rajasaḥ*, at the base of the region, he glosses as *lokasya mūle*, the root of the world — and identifies it with the altar. The cosmological phrase is read as a ritual location, which turns the verse from a statement about where fire sits in the universe into a statement about where it sits in the enclosure. Griffith keeps the cosmic reading, "at the region's base"; Wilson prints "at the root of the world" and lets it stand.

At verse 4 he takes *candram iva surucam* not as "like the moon" but as bright like gold, noting that *candra* in the neuter is a Vedic synonym for gold — and Wilson follows him with "resplendent as gold", where Griffith has "like the Moon waxing".

Verse 5's *hiriśipra* draws his longest gloss. *Śipra* he takes as chin or jaw, or else the nose; then, citing [[5.54]].11 on golden locks spread over the head, he allows *śipra* here to mean a turban or a curl. Wilson prints "blazing with radiant tresses", Griffith "Raging with jaws of gold" — the same word, and two quite different pictures of the fire.

On verse 10's *pañca kṛṣṭi* he is specific where the text is not, glossing the five peoples as the four *varṇas* plus the Niṣādas.

3.title: Āprī of the Gṛtsamadas — Eleven Called in Order
3.synthesis:
An Āprī hymn is not a hymn of praise. It is a sequence: eleven verses, and the Anukramaṇī gives each one a different addressee, in a fixed order that every family's Āprī keeps. What varies between them is the wording; what does not vary is the procession. This is the Gṛtsamada family's version, and reading it is like watching a rite from the door.

Verses 1 to 3 are {{agni}}, called three times over in three capacities. First he is *samiddha*, kindled, set down on the earth and standing facing all beings — *hotā pāvakaḥ pradivaḥ sumedhāḥ*, the caller, the purifier, the ancient, the wise — and the verse ends by asking the god to sacrifice to the gods: *devo devān yajatu*. Second (v2) he appears as {{narāśaṃsa}}, the one in whom men's praise is spoken, anointing the stations, bright through the three heavens, drenching the offering with a mind that pours *ghṛta*. Third (v3) he is *īḷita*, the invoked, asked to make the offering today *mānuṣāt pūrvaḥ*, ahead of the human priest, and to bring the {{marut}} troop and {{indra}} to sit on the grass.

Verse 4 addresses the *barhis* itself. The grass is *deva*, divine, and is spoken to: growing, rich in strong sons, strewn for wealth on this altar and wet with *ghṛta*. And then the invitation — sit down here, Vasus, all the {{viśvedevāḥ}}, all the Ādityas. A hymn to a handful of cut grass turns out to be the seating of the assembly.

Verse 5 is the doors: *dvāraḥ devīḥ*, goddesses, easy to pass, to be opened wide with *namas* — spread apart, undecaying, purifying the class that is famed and strong in men. Verse 6 is Uṣāsānaktā, dawn and night as a pair: like two skilled women weaving, they interweave in concert the thread that has been stretched, the ornament of the {{yajña}}, and they yield richly, full of milk. The rite is a fabric and the two halves of the day are working the loom.

Verse 7 gives the two divine *hotā*s — the first, the wiser, the more beautiful of form — worshipping straight with the *ṛc*, sacrificing *ṛtuthā*, in season, and anointing the gods at the navel of the earth on three high places. Verse 8 gives the three goddesses of speech: {{sarasvatī}}, who perfects our {{dhī}}; Iḷā; and {{bhāratī}}, all-surpassing — three goddesses seated by their own power, asked to protect this refuge without a flaw in it. Note the verb given to Sarasvatī alone: *sādhayantī dhiyaṃ naḥ*, making our thought work.

Verse 9 asks for a son and names him before he exists: tawny in colour, well borne, giving vitality, quick to hear, a hero, god-loving. {{tvaṣṭṛ}}, the shaper, is asked to loosen the navel-cord for us — to let the line continue — and then may the offering reach the gods' own pasture. Verse 10 is Vanaspati, the tree, standing near and releasing; Agni is to bring the offering to its right condition, neither under nor over; and the divine *śamitṛ*, the one who does the killing, is to carry forward what has been thrice anointed.

Verse 11 is the Svāhākṛtis, the calls that complete an oblation, and it is almost entirely one word: *ghṛtaṃ mimikṣe ghṛtam asya yoniḥ, ghṛte śrito ghṛtam u asya dhāma* — ghee is mixed, ghee is his womb, he rests in ghee, ghee is his dwelling. Four times in one line. Then the last instruction of the sequence: come as is your custom, bull, take pleasure, and carry the offering that has been consecrated with *svāhā*.
3.practice:
There are ten Āprī hymns in the Ṛgveda — [[1.13]], [[1.142]], [[1.188]], this one, [[3.4]], [[5.5]], [[7.2]], [[9.5]], [[10.70]] and [[10.110]] — one for each of the great priestly lines, and eight of the ten run to exactly eleven verses. That is what an Āprī is: a family's own wording for a fixed sequence, and the fixity is the point. The sequence belongs to the animal offering in the śrauta rites, where these verses are the *prayājas*, the fore-offerings that go before the main one. A reader who has never seen a śrauta sacrifice can still learn from this hymn what the tradition regards as the shape of an offering: kindle, call, seat, open, keep the time, purify the speech, ask for continuance, prepare the material, and close with *svāhā*.

Two things in it are still in daily use. The first is *svāhā* itself, verse 11's addressee — the syllable that concludes every oblation into fire, in a homa done today exactly as here. The second is the trio of verse 8. {{sarasvatī}}, Iḷā and {{bhāratī}} are invoked together as the three goddesses of speech and nourishment; the same three stand in the Āprī of every family, and Sarasvatī's assignment here — *sādhayantī dhiyaṃ naḥ*, perfecting our {{dhī}} — is the earliest statement of the office she never lost.

The verse a householder is likeliest to feel is the ninth. It asks for a son and describes him in advance, and then asks {{tvaṣṭṛ}}, the shaper of forms, to release the navel — to keep the line running. The Āprī is a hymn about a rite, and at its centre the concern is descent. Nothing in the tradition's later preoccupation with lineage is an innovation on this.

And verse 11 is worth reading aloud once for its sound alone. *Ghṛta* four times in a single line, as substance, as womb, as resting place, as dwelling. Clarified butter is not a garnish in the Vedic rite; it is the medium in which the whole exchange happens, and this line says so by refusing to use another word.
3.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa's note at verse 2 records a real structural difference between this Āprī and others. In the preceding Āprī hymns the second addressee is Tanūnapāt, a name of {{agni}}; here Tanūnapāt is omitted and {{narāśaṃsa}} takes the slot. He cross-refers to [[1.142]] and [[1.188]] as the comparison. The fixed sequence, in other words, is fixed with one known variable.

At verse 4 he notes that the *barhis*, addressed as a deity, is understood as a form of Agni — which is how a hymn can speak to cut grass without addressing an object.

Verse 7's three high places he identifies flatly as the three fires, *gārhapatya*, *āhavanīya* and *dakṣiṇā*, and the "navel of the earth" as the altar. Griffith keeps the language geographic — "three high places at the centre of the earth" — where Sāyaṇa reads a floor plan.

His most technical gloss is at verse 10, on *tridhā samaktam*, thrice anointed: he names the three acts as *upastaraṇa*, *avadāna* and *abhighāraṇa*, and reads *agnir haviḥ sūdayāti* as Agni cooking the offering to exactly the right point, neither underdone nor overdone. Wilson prints "fully dress the victim", Griffith the vaguer "with his arts prepare oblation".

At verse 11 he records an alternative construction in which the verse is addressed not to Agni but to the Adhvaryu, who is told to bring Agni to the oblation — and he notes the verse recurs at Yajurveda 17.88.

4.title: Agni Set Among Men by the Bhṛgus, Seen Burning
4.synthesis:
This sūkta and the three that follow — through [[2.7]] — are the only ones in this book the Anukramaṇī does not give to the Gṛtsamada line; they belong to Somāhuti Bhārgava, of the {{bhṛgu}} family. That shows in the second verse, where the poet names his own ancestors as the ones who put Agni in place — and it shows in the way this hymn looks at {{agni}}, which is less as an officiant than as a thing burning, watched closely by someone who cannot stop watching.

The first verse calls him for the assembly, not for the poet: *huve vaḥ*, I invoke on your behalf. Agni is *suvṛkti*, well-praised, the guest of the clans, well fed, and — the odd simile — *mitro iva yo didhiṣāyyo bhūt*, one to be won the way one wins a friend, a god among a god-seeking people, Jātavedas.

The second verse gives the family claim. The Bhṛgus, serving him, set him *dvitā*, in two places — in the meeting-place of the waters and among the settlements of man. Let him be over all the worlds, the *arati* of the gods with swift horses. The third verse repeats the placement from the gods' side: they set Agni among the human clans as a dear friend, as men do when they mean to settle somewhere; and he shines through the nights that want him, and shows his power in the house of the one who gives.

Then four verses of pure looking, and they are the best thing in the sūkta. Verse 4: his growth is as welcome as the growth of one's own goods; the sight of him when he is loosed and about to burn — he flings his tongue about among the plants *atyo na rathyo dodhavīti vārān*, like a harnessed racehorse shaking out its tail. Verse 5: he gave his colour, as it were, to those who wanted him; he is known by his bright, delightful blaze; and *jujurvān yo muhur ā yuvā bhūt* — having grown old, in a moment he is young again. That is a fire being fed, described exactly.

Verse 6: he lights up the forests like something thirsty; he roars like water down a channel, like a chariot on a road; *kṛṣṇādhvā*, his path is black behind him; hot, and delightful, and marked out like the sky smiling through cloud. Verse 7: he stands up and burns across the wide earth, and goes *paśur na svayur agopāḥ* — like an animal with no herdsman, going where it likes. Bright Agni, burning up the brushwood, leaving a black wound behind him, and it is as though he were seasoning the ground.

Then the sūkta remembers what it is for. Verse 8: this thought has been recited at the third *vidatha*, in remembrance of your earlier help; give us wealth with strong men in it, abundant, with good offspring. And verse 9 signs off with a name the family that finally kept this book will use again: *tvayā yathā gṛtsamadāso agne* — that through you the Gṛtsamadas, working unseen, may overcome those nearer them, rich in heroes and able to withstand attack; and to the patrons and to the singer, give that same vitality.

The hymn's real subject is in verses 4 to 7, and it is not doctrine. It is the observation that a fire behaves like a living animal — hungry, loose, ageing and renewing within a minute, leaving a black trail, needing no keeper. Nothing is asked of the reader except to look at it, and the asking is confined to the last two verses.
4.practice:
Maṇḍala 2 is the Gṛtsamada family's book, and 39 of its 43 sūktas are ascribed to that line. The four exceptions are this sūkta and the three after it, through [[2.7]], given to Somāhuti Bhārgava. That is a fact worth noticing rather than smoothing over: a family collection is not a sealed box. A Bhārgava's four Agni hymns sit inside it, near the front, and the ninth verse of this one names the Gṛtsamadas by name — which is how the seam was stitched.

{{agni}} is the god whose care the {{bhṛgu}} line claims. Verse 2 states it: the Bhṛgus set him *dvitā*, in the waters' place and among men's dwellings. The Bhṛgus are the lineage the tradition associates with the finding and the keeping of fire, and this verse is one of the collection's plainest assertions of that.

What the sūkta offers a reader now is its middle. Verses 4 to 7 are four verses of unhurried attention to what fire actually does — the tongue thrown about like a racehorse shaking its tail, the black path left behind, the roar like water down a slope, the animal loose without a herdsman, and the line that anyone who has sat by a hearth will recognise: *jujurvān yo muhur ā yuvā bhūt*, grown old, in a moment young again. That is not decoration. In a tradition where the deity of the *sandhyā* and of every saṃskāra is a fire that must be looked at while one recites, the discipline of actually watching it is part of the practice, and these four verses are a record of someone doing exactly that.

The eighth verse dates itself: *tṛtīye vidathe*, at the third gathering. The Vedic day carries three pressings — morning, midday and evening — and the poet is placing his recitation at the last of them, in memory of help given earlier. Ordinary praise, offered at a named hour. The Gṛtsamada name in verse 9 is one of only four occurrences of that family name anywhere in the Ṛgveda, and all four are in this book.
4.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa's coverage of this sūkta in the available witness is thin — three verses carry a gloss — and where he is silent that is a fact about the witness, not about him.

At verse 2 he explains *dvitā*, twice or in two places, as Agni made manifest in two forms: as lightning in the firmament, and as the cooking fire on earth. Wilson prints exactly that, "twice made him manifest"; Griffith keeps it temporal and vague, "set him of old in houses of the living", losing the two-places reading altogether.

At verse 3 he offers two constructions of *dīdayad uśatīr ūrmyāḥ*. Either the nights are the ones desiring — *uśatīḥ*, wished for — and Agni shines during them; or Agni lights up all the nights. Wilson chooses the first, "shines on the nights when he is wished for"; Griffith the second, "Against the longing nights may he shine brightly", which keeps the longing but reverses who is doing it.

Verse 5's first line is the sūkta's hardest, and the two translators do not agree on who is speaking. Wilson has the poet's colleagues extolling Agni's greatness; Griffith has Agni himself giving his colour to those who honour the speaker. The Sanskrit *ā yan me abhvaṃ vanadaḥ pananta* supports the ambiguity, and neither reading can be ruled out from the words alone.

5.title: Agni Takes Each Priest's Office — Potā, Neṣṭā, Ṛtvij
5.synthesis:
Eight short verses in *anuṣṭubh* — the only sūkta in maṇḍala 2 in that metre — and the whole of it is about who does what at a rite, and the discovery that one god is doing all of it. [[2.1]] made the same claim in a single crowded verse. Here it is unfolded slowly, one office at a time, and the effect is quite different: not a hymn of identification but a walk through the enclosure.

*Hotā ajaniṣṭa cetanaḥ* — the *hotā* has been born, the one who takes notice. Born as a father for the fathers, for their help, set to win noble wealth by the rite. And the first verse ends on an odd, honest request: *śakema vājino yamam* — may we be able to hold him, may we manage the reins of this strong one. {{agni}} arrives as an officiant and is immediately something that must be handled.

The second verse gives him the whole staff at once. In him, as *netṛ*, leader of the {{yajña}}, the seven reins are stretched out; and, human-fashion, he furthers all the divine work as *potā*, the purifier, eighth in the sequence. Seven and an eighth: the offices are being counted, and Agni is inside the count rather than above it.

The third verse says he needs no instruction. Whatever the officiant sets running, whatever formulations he speaks after — Agni knows them; and *nemiḥ cakram iva*, as the rim goes round the wheel, he has gone round every act of the wise. That image will be familiar from [[1.32]].15, where the felly encircling the spokes is what makes {{indra}} a king; here it is what makes a god competent at ritual — the same figure of holding a whole without crushing it.

The fourth verse makes the point that matters most in this sūkta. *Sākaṃ hi śucinā śuciḥ praśāstā kratunā ajani* — pure, he was born together with the pure act, as *praśāstā*, the director; and knowing this one's *vratāḥ*, the fixed observances, he grows up along them like branches along a stem. The god and the rite are not two things, one applied to the other. They were born at the same moment.

Verses 5 and 6 turn to the instruments and are deliberately domestic. The cows of the *neṣṭā* follow him, taking on his colour — the milk poured in, and the sisters, the fingers or the streams, that have come here. And when the sister vessel carrying *ghṛta* has taken her stand beside the mother, the *adhvaryu* rejoices at their arrival *yavo vṛṣṭīva*, as barley does at rain. That last comparison is worth stopping on. The priest's pleasure at the ghee arriving is the pleasure of a crop in a downpour: relief, not ceremony.

The seventh verse states the paradox baldly and does not blink. *Svaḥ svāya dhāyase kṛṇutām ṛtvig ṛtvijam* — let him make the *ṛtvij* an *ṛtvij* for his own nourishment; let the offering and the praise be prepared; then may we win, we have given. Agni is asked to officiate at a rite whose whole purpose is to feed Agni. He is priest, addressee and beneficiary at once, and the tradition sets this down as a fact rather than a puzzle.

The eighth closes with a modest wish that the human officiant should get it right: that this knowing one may do fit worship to all the adorable ones, and that the {{yajña}} we have made here should be *tve api*, in you as well. Eight verses to say that Agni is the priest, and the last line asks only that our work be found inside his.
5.practice:
This is the sūkta to read if the roster of Vedic priests has ever seemed like antiquarian furniture. It names them one after another — *hotā*, *netṛ*, *potā*, *praśāstā*, *neṣṭā*, *adhvaryu*, *ṛtvij* — and gives them all to {{agni}}. The great śrauta rites employ sixteen such officiants; the tradition's own count places eight of them in the first rank. What this hymn says is that the human division of labour is a copy. There is one office, and men take pieces of it.

That has a practical consequence a householder can use. A rite performed by one person before one fire is not a truncated version of a rite performed by sixteen. The seventh verse's paradox — *ṛtvig ṛtvijam*, the officiant made an officiant — states that Agni is doing the priestly work in either case. This is the theological ground beneath the fact that the Hindu domestic rites, the saṃskāras, are valid when the householder himself performs them.

*Ṛtvij* is the word to carry away, and it is worth taking apart once: *ṛtu* plus √yaj, one who offers at the proper season. Not the most learned man in the room — the one who acts when the time is right. The same *ṛtu* is named aloud in the *saṅkalpa* before any observance today, when the season and the moment are declared before anything else is said. The fourth verse of this sūkta says why that matters: Agni was born *sākaṃ kratunā*, together with the act. Timeliness is not a courtesy paid to a rite; it is the condition on which the god is present in it at all.

And verse 6 gives the image to hold. The *adhvaryu*, seeing the ghee-vessel set down beside the mother-vessel, is glad the way barley is glad in rain. The Ṛgveda has grander pictures of joy. It has few more accurate ones about what it feels like when a thing you have been preparing for finally begins.
5.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa reads this sūkta as a systematic assignment of priestly offices to {{agni}}, and says so at verse 1: here and in the following hymn Agni is addressed as identified with, or personified by, the several priests employed at sacrifices. That framing governs everything that follows, and Wilson's English is built on it — his rendering supplies the technical names in capitals throughout.

At verse 1 he takes *pitṛbhyaḥ* not as the ancestors but as *pālaka* or *yajamāna*, the patrons who institute the rite — so Wilson has "for the preservation of our patrons" where the word would as easily give "for the fathers". Griffith takes it as "our patrons' help" and so agrees, but the ancestral reading is not excluded by the Sanskrit.

Verse 2's seven reins he glosses as the seven priests engaged in their functions. Griffith keeps the image undecided — "the seven reins, far extended" — and leaves the reader to choose between rays, reins and men.

The largest divergence is at verse 5. Sāyaṇa and Wilson read the *neṣṭā*'s cows as the sister fingers that perform the pressing, combining through the three fires; Griffith reads a straightforward question instead — "Is he not better than the Three, the Sisters who have come to us?" One tradition sees ritual anatomy, the other a comparison. The words *kuvit tisṛbhya ā varam* support both.

6.title: Agni Given a Kindling-Stick and Asked to Listen
6.synthesis:
Eight verses of *gāyatrī*, the shortest metre, and the sūkta is correspondingly bare. There are no exploits in it and almost no cosmology. A man has brought fuel to a fire and is asking it to pay attention.

*Imāṃ me agne samidham imām upasadaṃ vaneḥ* — accept this kindling-stick of mine, this sitting-near of mine; and hear these songs, well. Three things are offered in the first verse and only one of them is a substance. The *samidh* is a piece of wood. The *upasad* is the act of sitting down close by. The *girā* are the words. The hymn puts them on the same footing and asks for all three to be taken.

The second verse names {{agni}} as *ūrjo napāt*, offspring of strength, and asks to serve him with this and with a well-made utterance, *sujāta*, well-born. The third is a small piece of word-play that is also the sūkta's argument: *taṃ tvā gīrbhir girvaṇasaṃ draviṇasyuṃ draviṇodaḥ, saparyema saparyavaḥ* — you who love songs, we honour with songs; you who want substance and give substance, we who want to honour, honour. Each half of the line matches the giver to what he wants. The exchange is not disguised, and there is no embarrassment in it.

The fourth verse asks for awareness and for defence in one breath: *sa bodhi* — be aware, be a *sūri*, a patron, *maghavan*, generous; lord of goods, giver of goods; and *yuyodhi asmad dveṣāṃsi*, keep the hatreds away from us. That last verb, *yuyodhi*, is the same one that ends the Īśa Upaniṣad's final prayer; here it is asked of Agni against enmity rather than against sin.

The fifth verse is three requests with nothing between them: he who gives us rain from heaven, he who gives us *vājam anarvāṇam*, strength that nothing can overtake, he who gives us food by the thousand. Rain, unassailable strength, abundance — the whole material ambition of a household in one verse, addressed to a fire.

The sixth changes tone. *Īḷānāya avasyave yaviṣṭha dūta naḥ girā, yajiṣṭha hotar ā gahi* — to the one praising, to the one wanting help, come, youngest, our messenger, best sacrificer, *hotā*. Two words there are worth holding. *Yaviṣṭha*, youngest, is a standing epithet of Agni because a fire is newborn each time it is struck; and *dūta*, messenger, is the office on which the whole system depends — a god who is not the destination but the road.

The seventh verse explains why he can hold that office. *Antar hi agne īyase vidvāṃ janmobhayā kave* — you go between, knowing both births, both kinds, the gods' and men's, like a messenger who is at home among a people and bound to them by friendship. He is not neutral. He knows both sides and is a *mitrya*, a friend, on both.

The eighth ends where such a hymn should. Knowing all this, gladden us; worship in the right order, *ānuṣak*, one after another without a gap; and sit down here on this *barhis*. Nothing has been asked that a man could not ask on an ordinary evening, and the last thing requested is simply that the god should sit down.
6.practice:
The *samidh* in the first line is the point of contact between this sūkta and a life now. Placing a stick of wood in a fire with a mantra is the simplest complete Vedic act there is, and it survives intact: the *samidādhāna* is the daily obligation of the brahmacārin, morning and evening, and the *samidh* offering opens a homa of any scale. This hymn is what such an act sounds like from the inside. It brings wood, and sitting close, and words — and asks that all three be accepted, without distinguishing the material offering from the attention.

*Upasad*, the second of the three, is the word to notice. It means sitting down near, and it is offered here as though it were a substance. The tradition never lost that sense: *upāsanā*, the ordinary word for worship, is the same root and the same idea — being near, staying near. The Ṛgveda's word for what a person brings to a fire is not belief and not feeling. It is proximity, sustained.

Verse 4's *yuyodhi asmad dveṣāṃsi* — keep the hatreds away from us — is a line a reader may already know in another shape. The same imperative stands in [[1.189]].1 — *yuyodhy asmaj juhurāṇam eno*, keep the crooked fault away from us — the verse the Īśa Upaniṣad takes over as its own last words, addressed to Agni there too. The phrase *yuyodhi asmat* occurs five times in the Ṛgveda, three of them to Agni. The verb and the addressee are constant across a thousand years of the tradition; only the thing to be kept off has changed, from other men's malice to one's own fault. That drift is one of the more instructive things a reader can watch in the corpus.

And verse 7 states the reason {{agni}} rather than another god stands at the front of nearly every collection. *Antar īyase*, you travel between, *vidvān janmobhayā*, knowing both kinds of birth. Not a god above the transaction but one inside it, at home in both houses. That is the whole logic of a mediator, and the Ṛgveda gives it in a single *gāyatrī* line.
6.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa's glosses here are short and lexical, and two of them change the sense of a whole verse.

At verse 2 the compound *aśvamiṣṭe* is genuinely obscure and he offers two routes: a rite that is expansive, *vyāpaka yajña*, or else from *āśu*, quick — one who desires prompt worship. Wilson takes the second, "gratified by prompt sacrifice"; Griffith reads the first element as *aśva* and gets "seeker of horses", a quite different god.

At verse 4 he reads the imperative *bodhi* as understanding rather than shining, and supplies an object — *abhimatam*, our wish — so Wilson has "understand (our prayers)". Griffith drops the verb's cognitive sense entirely: "Be thou for us a liberal Prince." He also records that this verse recurs at Yajurveda 12.43.

At verse 6 he separates the two epithets carefully: *īḷāna* is the one doing the worshipping, and *avasyu* is glossed *svarakṣaṇam icchate*, one who wants his own preservation — the request is not disinterested and the gloss does not pretend otherwise.

The two translators also part on verse 3. Wilson makes Agni *draviṇodas*, the giver of substance, the addressee of the whole line; Griffith reads the same word as vocative-and-adjective together, "wealth-lover, giver of our wealth", keeping the mirroring of desire that the Sanskrit builds.

23.title: Brahmaṇaspati as Gaṇapati; Bṛhaspati on Guard
23.synthesis:
*Gaṇānāṃ tvā gaṇapatiṃ havāmahe* — we call on you, the gaṇapati of the gaṇas. The line is probably the most widely recited half-verse in this maṇḍala, and the god it calls is {{brahmaṇaspati}}. Three more titles follow in the same verse: *kaviṃ kavīnām*, the seer among seers; *upamaśravastamam*, of renown beyond comparison; *jyeṣṭharājaṃ brahmaṇām*, chief king of the {{brahman}}s — the formulated words that make a rite work. Then the request, which is small: hearing us, come with your helps and sit down in our seat.

Nineteen verses follow, and the name alternates. Six of them address him as Brahmaṇaspati and thirteen as {{bṛhaspati}}, and the hymn moves between the two without marking the change. The second verse makes the largest claim in the sūkta: even the discerning gods obtained their sacrificial share through him, and as Sūrya generates the rays by his light, so he alone is *janitā*, begetter, of all the *brahman*s. The third mounts him on a chariot — *jyotiṣmantaṃ rathaṃ ṛtasya*, the shining chariot of {{ṛta}} — and loads it with what it does: terrible, humbler of foes, killer of rakṣas, splitter of the cow-pen, finder of the light.

The fourth and fifth verses state the protection in its plainest form. He leads men by *sunīti*, good guidance; no *aṃhas*, no narrow distress, reaches the one who gives to him; and he burns the *brahmadviṣ*, the man who hates the sacred word. The fifth lists four things that cannot get past him — sorrow, misfortune, hostility, the double-tongued — for whoever he guards as *sugopā*, a good herdsman. The sixth calls him *pathikṛt*, maker of the road, and asks that the deceiver's own malice be what grinds him down. The seventh asks that the arrogant man who attacks the guiltless be turned off our path and the road to this offering be made easy. The eighth is the most intimate: *trātāraṃ tanūnām*, protector of our bodies, and *adhivaktāram*, one who speaks on our behalf.

Verses nine through thirteen turn outward again. Through him may we take the desirable goods of men, and may the hostile near and far be crushed (v9); through him may we hold the highest vigour, and let no ill-speaking man rule us (v10); he is *ananudaḥ*, who yields to none, going to the battle-cry, victorious, true, *ṛṇayā*, the exactor of debts, tamer even of the fierce (v11); let the weapon of the man who plots against us not reach us (v12); he is to be called in battles and approached with *namas*, and he overturns the malignant like chariots (v13).

The last movement returns to speech. Burn the rakṣas who held your proven strength in scorn, and *āvis tat kṛṣva yad asat te ukthyam* — make visible that in you which will deserve the hymn (v14). Born of ṛta, give us the wealth that shines among men (v15). Do not hand us to thieves who covet another's food and harbour the abandonment of the gods in their hearts — men who *na paraḥ sāmno viduḥ*, know nothing beyond the sāman (v16). {{tvaṣṭṛ}} generated him above all beings, poet of every sāman, exactor and discharger of debt, slayer of injury, in the upholding of great ṛta (v17). And once, for his glory, the mountain opened, the pen of cows was released, and with {{indra}} as yoke-fellow he poured out the flood of waters that darkness had wrapped (v18).

The nineteenth asks him to be *yantṛ* of this very hymn — its guide — and to quicken our offspring; then the closing line the family sets at the end of most of what it composes. What runs through all nineteen verses is *brahman*: he is king of it in verse 1, father of it in verse 2, and the man who hates it is what he burns in verse 4. This is a god whose weapon is the formulated word.
23.practice:
The first line of this sūkta is recited daily across India, and almost always without its second half. It is worth knowing exactly what it says. *Gaṇapati* occurs precisely twice in the Ṛgveda: here, of {{brahmaṇaspati}}, and at [[10.112]].9, where it is said to {{indra}}. Neither verse concerns Gaṇeśa, who does not appear in the Ṛgveda at all. The tradition that later attached this line to him is a real tradition and a very old one, but the Ṛgvedic address is to the lord of the sacred word, and the hymn that follows spends nineteen verses on protection, debt and speech.

The second half of the verse is the part worth recovering: *jyeṣṭharājaṃ brahmaṇāṃ brahmaṇaspata ā naḥ śṛṇvann ūtibhiḥ sīda sādanam* — chief king of the sacred formulations, Brahmaṇaspati, hearing us, sit down in our seat with your helps. That is why the line opens ceremonies. It is not a general auspicious noise; it is a request that the power behind correct speech take a seat where the speaking is about to happen.

{{bṛhaspati}} and Brahmaṇaspati between them are named as the deity of twenty-two sūktas across the collection, and four of those stand consecutively here — [[2.23]], [[2.24]], [[2.25]] and [[2.26]] — the largest single block given to him anywhere. Whoever assembled this family book placed him immediately after the long Indra sequence, and the placement reads as deliberate: the god who breaks by force, then the god who breaks by *{{brahman}}*.

Two things in the hymn bear directly on ordinary life. The first is *ṛṇayā*, exactor of debts, at verses 11 and 17, with *ṛṇacit* beside it — the sense that obligations are tracked and eventually settled, and that this is a divine function rather than a social one. The second is verse 8's *adhivaktā*, the one who speaks on your behalf. For a household whose difficulties are with what other people say — slander, false accusation, a reputation under attack — this hymn is the address the Ṛgveda supplies, and the request in verse 8 is not for victory but for an advocate.
23.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa derives Brahmaṇaspati from *brahman* in two senses at once and does not choose: protector of *anna*, food, or of the great and solemn act of devotion. For Bṛhaspati he suggests *bṛhatāṃ vedānām pālakaḥ*, keeper of the great mantras, and remarks that Bṛhaspati is the more martial of the two, invoked against enemies and evil spirits — an observation the hymn's own distribution of the two names does not obviously bear out.

Verse 1's *upamaśravastama* splits the translators badly. Wilson prints "abounding beyond measure in every kind of food"; Griffith has "the famousest of all". The compound is built on *śravas*, renown, and Griffith is closer to the surface of the word.

Verse 16's *na paraḥ sāmno viduḥ* draws Sāyaṇa's fullest note here: he takes it to mean those who know nothing higher than the rakṣas-destroying power derived from you, citing the maxim *sāma vai rakṣohā*, the sāman is the killer of rakṣas. Wilson follows him; Griffith reads it quite differently — "no further rest shall they obtain."

On verse 17 Sāyaṇa offers two constructions of *sāmnaḥ sāmnaḥ kaviḥ*: either Brahmaṇaspati is the reciter of every sāman, or *kavi* refers to Tvaṣṭṛ, who produced him by the potency of the sāman. He glosses *ṛṇacit* as one who treats the praiser's intention as a debt owed, and *ṛṇayā* as the remover of the debt that is sin.
23.note: gaṇapati verified as occurring at exactly 2.23.1 and 10.112.9 across all ten padapāṭha files; the Brahmaṇaspati/Bṛhaspati alternation across the 19 verses counted from the padapāṭha and agrees with the Anukramaṇī; the 22-sūkta figure counted from all ten Anukramaṇī files

24.title: Brahmaṇaspati Splits Vala by Brahman, Not by Bolt
24.synthesis:
The hymn's whole argument sits in one word of its third verse, and everything else in the sixteen serves it.

It opens quietly. Accept this offering, you who rule; we will serve you with this new and mighty song; as this friend of yours, our patron, praises you, fulfil our thought (v1). The second verse begins the exploits: he bent down what was to be bent by his strength, tore open the strongholds of Śambara in his fury, dislodged the immovable, and entered the mountain full of goods. That is Indra's résumé, given to {{brahmaṇaspati}}.

Then the third verse. *Ud gā ājad abhinad brahmaṇā valam* — he drove up the cows, and he split Vala **by *{{brahman}}***. Not with a bolt; with the formulated word. The verse frames it as the greatest deed done for the godliest of the gods: what was fastened came loose, what was firm gave way, the darkness was hidden and the light displayed. The fourth continues the opening of what was shut — the well with a mouth of stone pouring honey, which he tore open by his strength, and all who see the light have drunk their fill of it.

The fifth verse is the hymn's strangest and gentlest: months and autumns pass, the doors open of themselves, and without effort the two go on exchanging one thing for another, in the knowledge-orders that Brahmaṇaspati established. Then the story of the search. Verses 6 and 7 belong together: the sages, seeking on every side, reached the Paṇis' furthest treasure hidden in the cave; and having seen through the falsehoods for what they were, they turned back to where they had come from and pressed their way in again. The seventh names what they carried — with their two arms they cast on the rock Agni that had not been there before. Discovery here is not a single stroke but a return: they had to go back over the ground once.

The eighth arms him. With a bow strung with *{{ṛta}}* and quick to loose, he hits whatever he intends; and his arrows are *nṛcakṣasaḥ karṇayonayaḥ* — meant for the eyes of men, and born from the ear. The ninth gathers his offices: he brings together and he separates, he is *purohita*, the one set in front; he is well praised; in battle he is Brahmaṇaspati; and when he brings out prize and treasure for the hymn, the sun burns without effort.

The tenth and eleventh are about scale. His attainable gifts are first and pre-eminent, and both classes of people live off them (v10); he has grown great by his own strength, spread wide toward the gods, and encompasses everything (v11). The twelfth is the only verse addressed to a pair — Indra and Brahmaṇaspati together, from whom all truth proceeds, whose *vrata* not even the waters transgress: come to our oblation as yoked steeds come to fodder.

The last four return to the assembly hall. The swiftest bearers hear the call; the *vipra* fit for the assembly wins wealth by his thought; hard on the hostile, remitting the debt as he chooses, he is the strong one in the clash (v13). His purpose took effect exactly as he wished when he had a great deed to do — he drove up the cows and shared them out to heaven, and they ran apart in strength like a great river (v14). May we be masters of well-governed, life-bearing wealth; add heroes to our heroes, since you, having power, come to my call through *brahman* (v15). And the sixteenth is verse for verse identical with the closing verse of [[2.23]]: be the guide of this hymn, quicken our offspring, all is good that the gods favour.

*Brahman* stands in twelve of the sixteen verses. It is the bow, the entry, the weapon and the summons.
24.practice:
This is the sūkta that tells you what the Ṛgveda thought a mantra was for. The Vala story is told three or four times in the collection, and it is normally {{indra}}'s: a hidden pen, cows shut inside, a stroke, a release. Here the pen is opened by *{{brahman}}* — verse 3, *brahmaṇā valam*, in the instrumental. The formulated word is the instrument that does the work a weapon does elsewhere.

That is the ground of a very large later claim. When the tradition holds that a correctly formed and correctly uttered mantra is efficacious — not a request that something be done but the doing of it — this verse is among the oldest places it can point. And the same hymn hedges it: verse 8 makes his arrows *karṇayonayaḥ*, born from the ear. Speech that has been heard properly is the ammunition. Nothing here works without the transmission being intact.

Verses 6 and 7 are the ones to keep for study. The seekers reach the treasure, see through the falsehoods, and then *punar ā ataḥ ā tasthuḥ* — they go back and stand on the great roads again, and only then get in. The Ṛgveda's picture of finding something out involves a second pass over ground already covered. It also involves company: they are plural throughout, *kavayaḥ*, and no one of them does it alone.

For observance, note that {{brahmaṇaspati}} is the deity of the *brahman* priest, the one who sits silent and watches the whole rite for error. Verse 9 gives him the title *purohita*, placed in front, which the tradition later attaches to the household priest, and verse 13 has him remitting a debt at his own discretion — *ṛṇam ādadiḥ*. Together with [[2.23]].11 and 17 that makes debt one of this block's steady preoccupations, and it is not a metaphor: the Ṛgveda's word for a discharged obligation is the same word a householder uses.
24.disagreements:
The reading of the whole hymn turns on whether the cows are cows. Sāyaṇa states the allegory plainly at verse 6: the cows hidden in the caves are the rains accumulated in the clouds, set free by oblations with fire, of which the Aṅgirasas were the authors. Wilson follows that into English at verse 4, where the "stone-like, solid, down-hanging, water-laden cloud" is entirely his commentator's; Griffith keeps the well of stone that "poured a flood of meath" and lets it stand.

Verse 5 is unsettled in both directions. Sāyaṇa reads *bhuvanā bhavītvā* as the waters that are to be, and takes the two who exchange without effort as heaven and earth — rain engendered above, fertility below, food offered, rain again, a perpetual interchange sustained by prayer. Griffith renders the same verse as creatures, moons and autumns, and doors that open of themselves; the two English versions barely resemble each other.

At verse 7, Sāyaṇa takes *nakiḥ so asti* to mean the fire was simply not there before — the sages produced by their own power a fire that did not exist and threw it on the rock — and reads the line as an allusion to the spread of fire-worship by the Aṅgirasas. On verse 8's arrows he is brief and striking: the first sort are oblations, obvious to the sight, and the second are mantras, addressed to the ears of men.
24.note: brahman counted in 12 of 16 verses from the padapāṭha; brahmaṇā at v3 confirmed instrumental singular from the morphology file; 2.24.16 verified word-for-word identical with 2.23.19

25.title: Five Verses on Whom Brahmaṇaspati Takes as Ally
25.synthesis:
Five verses, and every one of them ends with the same line: *yaṃ-yaṃ yujaṃ kṛṇute brahmaṇas patiḥ* — whomever, whomever {{brahmaṇaspati}} makes his yoke-fellow. The doubled *yaṃ-yaṃ* is not decoration; it means each one, any one, whoever it happens to be. The hymn is a single sentence with its subject deferred five times, and the effect on a reciter is cumulative: four fresh promises, and then, at the end of each, the one condition on which all of them hang.

The first verse begins with a man at a fire. Kindling {{agni}}, he shall overcome those who would overcome him; having made his *{{brahman}}*, having given his oblation, he shall thrive; and *jātena jātam ati sa pra sarsṛte* — by what is born of him he spreads out past what is born of another. Not that his rivals fail, but that his line goes further than theirs.

The second stays with descendants and turns them into force: with heroes he overcomes hostile heroes; he spreads out *{{rayi}}* by cattle; he knows *tmanā*, of himself, without being told; and his children and his children's children grow. The third leaves the household for three images of unstoppable motion — like the Sindhu tearing at what stands in its way, like a bull against oxen, and *agner iva prasitir nāha vartave*, like the onrush of fire, which cannot be turned back. That last is worth pausing on: fire is the one thing in this hymn's world that no amount of strength stops, and it is chosen to describe an ordinary man's momentum.

The fourth turns the sky on. For him the heavenly waters run unfailing; first among the strong he goes out after cattle; his vigour not blunted, he strikes with force. And the fifth ends where a Vedic hymn about prosperity generally does not: not with the man's action but with what surrounds him. For him all the rivers roar down; unbroken shelters, many of them, have been set about him; and *devānāṃ sumne subhagaḥ sa edhate* — in the favour of the gods, fortunate, he thrives. The verbs have changed hands. In verses 1 to 4 the man is the one doing things; in verse 5 everything is being done for him.

The two verbs of the opening — *vanavad vanuṣyataḥ*, he shall overcome those who would overcome him — recur in verse 2 and again in the first verse of [[2.26]], which is otherwise a different hymn to the same god. Across the whole Ṛgveda that phrase occurs four times, and three of them are here. These two short sūktas were made as a pair, and they are asking the same question from two ends: this one asks what happens to the man Brahmaṇaspati chooses, and [[2.26]] asks what a man does to be chosen.

What the refrain refuses to say is why he chooses. There is no test named, no offering specified, no lineage required. The hymn describes a river, a bull, a fire and a growing family, and then hands all of it over to a decision it does not explain.
25.practice:
This is the shortest complete argument in the maṇḍala and the easiest to memorise: five verses, one refrain, and a picture of a prospering household that a reciter can hold entire.

Its interest for a life is the shape of what it promises. The goods named are the ordinary Vedic ones — sons, grandsons, cattle, rain, *{{rayi}}*. What is unusual is the grammar of the last verse, where the man stops acting and is acted upon: rivers roar for him, shelters are set around him, he thrives in the gods' *sumna*. The hymn describes effort for four verses and then describes what effort by itself does not produce.

The refrain names the relation as *yuj*, yoke-fellow — the same root behind *yoga* and behind the *yukta* of later usage. It is not devotee, not servant, not son. It is the animal harnessed on the other side of the same pole, doing the same work in the same direction. That is a specific and demanding image of what a relation with a god was thought to be, and it is worth setting beside [[2.23]].8, where the same god is asked to be *adhivaktā*, the one who speaks on your behalf.

Read this with [[2.26]] immediately after; the two share their opening phrase and were plainly meant to stand together. Together with [[2.23]] and [[2.24]] they form the largest concentration of Brahmaṇaspati material anywhere in the Ṛgveda — four consecutive sūktas, of the twenty-two in the whole collection that name him or {{bṛhaspati}}. Nothing before or after gathers him like this. If a reader wants to know who the lord of the sacred word was to the people who composed for him, these four are where to go.
25.disagreements:
Wilson and Griffith divide on who is doing what. Wilson supplies "the worshipper" as the subject of the first verse and reads the closing line as a relative clause describing him, so that the man kindles, prays, offers and prospers, and Brahmaṇaspati appears only at the end. Griffith keeps the same structure but reads verse 1's *jātena jātam ati* as seed and seed — "he with his seed spreads forth beyond another's seed" — where Wilson, following his commentator, has him live to see the son of his son. Both are defensible from the words; the second is the softer.

Verse 3 is where they part hardest. Wilson makes the river the image of a man washing away his banks and the devout worshipper the one who overpowers; Griffith reads the man himself as "mighty like a raving river's billowy flood". The line's actual subject is unexpressed and both are supplying it.

The Sāyaṇa material available here is thin — a single gloss, and it belongs to a phrase of [[2.26]].3 rather than to this hymn, explaining *pitaram* as *pālayitāram*, protector or cherisher, where Brahmaṇaspati is called the father of the gods. Absence of a gloss in this witness is not evidence that the tradition was silent about the sūkta.
25.note: the refrain verified present in all five verses of the padapāṭha and nowhere else in the Ṛgveda; vanavad vanuṣyataḥ verified at 2.25.1, 2.25.2, 2.26.1 and 9.77.4 only

26.title: Brahmaṇaspati Rewards the Straight Praiser
26.synthesis:
Four verses, and they answer the question [[2.25]] left open. That hymn described what becomes of the man {{brahmaṇaspati}} takes as yoke-fellow and never said how a man comes to be taken. This one begins from the other end.

*Ṛjur ic chaṃsaḥ* — the straight praise, the straight praiser. He shall overcome those who would overcome him; the one who seeks the gods shall get the better of the godless; the one who wins favour shall overcome in battles the man who cannot be overcome; and the one who sacrifices shall take for himself the food of the one who does not. Four clauses in one verse, all of the same shape: a man with one quality set against a man without it, and the first prevails. And the quality that opens the list is not power or wealth but *ṛju* — straightness. The first word of the hymn is the answer to its predecessor.

The second verse turns from the third person to the second and speaks to a man directly. *Yajasva vīra* — sacrifice, hero; drive off those who plot; make your mind *bhadra*, good and firm, for the overcoming of obstruction; prepare the oblation so that you may be fortunate. Then, in the same breath, the speaker steps out of the instruction and back into the congregation: *brahmaṇas pater avaḥ ā vṛṇīmahe* — we choose the help of Brahmaṇaspati. The advice was to act; the last quarter of the verse admits that acting is not enough.

The third names the reward and, unusually, names it socially. He wins *{{vāja}}* and wealth *janena*, with his people; *viśā*, with his clan; *janmanā*, by his birth; *putraiḥ*, with his sons; *nṛbhiḥ*, along with the men. Five expressions for the same thing, which is that nothing here is won alone. And the man who does the winning is described in one phrase: *śraddhāmanāḥ*, of believing mind, who with an oblation serves Brahmaṇaspati, called here *devānāṃ pitaram*, father of the gods.

The fourth is the shortest and the most personal. Whoever has served him with offerings rich in ghee — *pra taṃ prācā nayati brahmaṇas patiḥ*, Brahmaṇaspati leads that man forward, on ahead. Then three verbs of rescue in a row: *uruṣyati*, he gives him room, out of *aṃhas*, the narrow place; *rakṣati riṣaḥ*, he guards him from injury; and even out of *aṃhu*, tight straits, he is for that man *urucakri*, the maker of wide space, *adbhuta*, beyond expectation.

That last epithet is where the pair of hymns lands. *Uru* against *aṃhas* — width against narrowness — is one of the Ṛgveda's oldest ways of saying rescue, and here it is the closing word about a god whose domain is speech. The straight praiser of verse 1 is not promised victory in any grand sense. He is promised room to stand in.
26.practice:
Four verses, and the first word of the first is the one to carry: *ṛju*, straight. The hymn's whole account of what makes a man's approach effective begins there, before any mention of offering, wealth or descent. *Ṛju* is the ordinary word for an unbent stick or an undeviating road, and its opposite in this hymn's second verse is not weakness but *manāyat*, the man who is calculating something.

Verse 3 is the one to weigh against a modern reading habit. It says the man of *śraddhā* wins his prize *janena*, *viśā*, *janmanā*, *putraiḥ*, *nṛbhiḥ* — with his people, his clan, his birth, his sons, the men around him. Five ways of saying that the reward is not individual. The Ṛgveda has almost no vocabulary for private good fortune; what a man receives here arrives attached to everyone he is attached to.

*Śraddhā* itself is worth marking. The word that carries the whole weight of later devotional vocabulary appears in this hymn as *śraddhāmanāḥ*, of trusting mind, and it is the single named qualification of the successful worshipper. It is not knowledge and not correctness of procedure. Both of those matter elsewhere in this block — [[2.24]] makes the *{{brahman}}* itself the instrument that splits Vala — but here what is asked for is trust.

The fourth verse gives the practical shape of what is expected of the god, and it is modest. Not conquest: *uruṣyati aṃhasaḥ*, he makes room out of the narrow place. The pair *uru* / *aṃhas*, width against constriction, recurs throughout the collection as the basic image of being helped, and it survives in ordinary speech: to be in *saṅkaṭa* is to be in a tight spot, and what is asked of the god is space. Read this immediately after [[2.25]], with which it shares its opening phrase; the two were made as a pair and neither is complete without the other.
26.disagreements:
No gloss for this sūkta survives in the Sāyaṇa witness available here — the file carries nothing for 2.26 at all. That is a gap in this witness and not evidence that the commentator passed the hymn over; his note on *devānāṃ pitaram*, father of the gods, glossed as *pālayitāram*, protector or cherisher, is filed against [[2.25]] but plainly belongs to verse 3 of this hymn, which is where the phrase occurs.

Verse 1 divides the translators over how much is being claimed. Wilson keeps supplying Brahmaṇaspati as the implied object throughout — "the sincere praiser of Brahmaṇaspati", "the propitiator of Brahmaṇaspati" — where the Sanskrit has only the adjectives standing alone. Griffith leaves them bare: "The righteous singer shall o'ercome his enemies, and he who serves the Gods subdue the godless man." Griffith is closer to the words; Wilson is transmitting how the tradition read them in context.

The second verse's *vṛtratūrye* is the one real crux. Wilson takes it generally — "in contending against foes" — while Griffith has "for the fight with foes". Neither prints the proper name, though the compound is built on *vṛtra*, and the same word elsewhere in the collection carries the specific sense of overcoming the obstruction that {{indra}} overcomes. Whether an ordinary man's battle is being described in Indra's vocabulary, or only in a dead metaphor of it, the evidence here does not settle.
26.note: sayana-mandala-2.json carries no entry for sūkta 26; the single gloss filed under 2.25 addresses a phrase that occurs at 2.26.3
